detail: When a native gate exceeds its timeout, gate.py SIGTERMs the process group and closes the pipe while the output-streaming thread is still blocked in read(), which raises ValueError: I/O operation on closed file. Because that happens last, it becomes the final thing in the job log, so a gate that timed out is presented as a crash inside the harness. macos-swiftui failed exactly this way: the appium smoke was Terminated at its timeout and the real cause sat two hundred lines above a Python traceback pointing at gate.py. The verdict was never wrong, since execute() already returned timed-out and the gate still failed, so this is an attribution defect rather than a correctness one. Attribution is the product's whole business: a criu restore hang that read as a product regression cost a full investigation the same day, and a harness that blames itself for a child's timeout is that mistake pointed inward. The read now returns on a closed stream instead of raising. HONEST LIMIT: the CI race did not reproduce on this machine, where a timed-out child returns timed-out with and without the guard, so the local check proves the timeout path still reports correctly and NOT that it reproduces the traceback. The guard is correct by construction, a closed pipe having nothing left to stream, rather than proven against the failure it was written for. FOLLOW-UP, same file: process-capsule-longrun and process-checkpoint share one script and differ only by REPROIT_CHECKPOINT_SCOPE, which the workflow set on the command line while the gate entry also declared it in an 'environment' block that gate.py never read. Invoking the narrow gate by name alone therefore ran the wide harness and failed its requiredOutput. gate.py now applies a gate's declared environment to the child, so the declaration is authoritative and the workflow does not have to remember the variable. A declaration the runner ignores is the same failure as a gate that cannot be scheduled: it reads as configuration and behaves as nothing.
